name: Aphrodisias
desc: A marble city in a poplar-shaded valley, quarried from the hillside above it, so the carving is everywhere: the stadium seats thirty thousand and is the best preserved anywhere, the Tetrapylon stands re-erected, and the Sebasteion reliefs in the museum show Claudius wrestling Britannia. Sheep still graze between the fallen column drums.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter mornings are foggy and the valley floods
tip: Do the museum first so you recognise where the Sebasteion panels came from, then walk the loop anticlockwise to reach the stadium before the coaches from Pamukkale arrive at eleven.
todo: Walk the full length of the stadium
rev: Repeat visitors rate it above Ephesus for atmosphere because there is space to breathe, though the site is large, shadeless in the middle hours and the last stretch of road from the Denizli highway is slow.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) or İzmir (ADB), then roughly 2 hours by road via Karacasu; there is no useful bus, so hire a car

name: Priene
desc: A Hellenistic grid city on a terrace under a 370-metre cliff, laid out by the same planners who drew Rhodes. Five columns of the Temple of Athena stand against pine and rock, the little bouleuterion still has its stone benches on four sides, and the streets are cobbled and steep. The Meander plain stretches flat below.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the climb from the car park is punishing in July
tip: Sit in the theatre's five marble thrones in the front row, then keep walking uphill past the temple to the west gate where nobody goes and the whole grid opens out below you.
rev: Visitors love the pine shade and the emptiness compared with Ephesus, and consistently warn that the stepped approach path is a real climb and that there is no café or shade at the top.
onward: İzmir (ADB) or Bodrum (BJV), then road to Söke and 15 km west to Güllübahçe; buses run Söke–Güllübahçe but drop you at the village, not the gate

name: Miletus
desc: The city that invented Western philosophy now sits in a cotton field four miles from the sea it once ruled, its harbour silted solid by the Meander. The Roman theatre is enormous and you can climb through its vaulted passages to the Byzantine castle on top. Storks nest on the İlyas Bey Mosque next door.
season: Apr–May and Oct — the plain is a mosquito swamp after rain and an oven in August
tip: Walk five minutes to the İlyas Bey Mosque of 1404, a perfect little Menteşe-era building with a marble portal, that most day-trippers drive straight past.
todo: Climb the theatre vaults to the castle
İlyas Bey Mosque and its storks
rev: People find the scale of the theatre astonishing and the rest of the site confusing and waterlogged; the ground is often muddy and the small museum is frequently shut without notice.
onward: Bodrum (BJV) or İzmir (ADB), then the Söke–Didim road; Miletus, Priene and Didyma are a natural one-day loop by car

name: Didyma
desc: Two complete columns nineteen metres high, and behind them a temple platform you descend into by a sloping tunnel to reach the oracle courtyard where the laurel grew. The Medusa head lying at ground level is the photograph everyone takes. The scale is closer to a cathedral than a temple and it was never finished.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the marble throws heat back at you in midsummer
tip: Go through the vaulted ramp on the north side into the inner court rather than only circling the outside; that descent is the whole point of the building.
todo: Descend the vaulted ramp to the adyton
rev: Almost everyone calls it the most impressive single ruin on this coast, then notes the ring of souvenir shops and carpet touts pressed right up against the fence and a car park that fills with coaches by ten.
onward: Bodrum (BJV) about 1 hr 15 by road, or İzmir (ADB) about 2 hr 30; town dolmuşes from Altınkum stop at the temple gate

name: Altınkum
desc: A shallow, gold-sand bay with water that stays waist-deep for fifty metres, which is why every Turkish family with small children ends up here. The promenade is fish restaurants, ice cream and British bars in equal measure. Walk west past the marina to Cengiz Topel and the beaches thin out fast.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for the town without the crowd
tip: Skip the main strip and take the coast road west to Akbük or south to Tavşan Burnu, where the same water comes without the loudspeakers.
todo: Swim off the shallow main beach
Fish supper on the marina front
rev: Families rate the safe shallow water highly; almost every review mentions that July and August bring package crowds, sunbed charges and traffic on the single beach road.
entry: Free · sunbed and umbrella hire extra
onward: Bodrum (BJV) about 1 hr 15 by road, or İzmir (ADB) 2 hr 30; frequent buses from Söke and Aydın otogar

name: Kuşadası
desc: A cruise port with an old quarter that survives behind it: Kaleiçi's grid of low stone houses, the Öküz Mehmet Pasha caravanserai of 1618 on the harbour, and a bazaar street that turns genuinely good the further uphill you climb. Two ships in port changes the town completely for six hours, then it empties.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August is hot, full and expensive
tip: Check the cruise schedule board at the port; on a no-ship day the bazaar prices and the pressure from shop callers drop by half.
rev: Handy as a base for Ephesus and Priene and praised for its seafront, but reviewers are blunt about aggressive shop touts on Barbaros Hayrettin street and the wall of cruise passengers on double-ship days.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB) about 1 hr 15 by road; regular buses from İzmir otogar and Selçuk, and a summer ferry from Samos

name: Pigeon Island
desc: A rock islet joined to Kuşadası by a 350-metre causeway, ringed by a low Ottoman sea wall with a small keep in the middle. Inside there are figs, cats, a tea garden and a circular walk of ten minutes that puts the whole bay and the Greek island of Samos in front of you.
season: Apr–Nov — the causeway takes spray in winter storms
tip: Come an hour before sunset and walk the seaward side of the wall, not the tea-garden side; the light hits the fortress and the fishing boats come back at the same time.
rev: A cheap and genuinely pleasant half hour, though visitors note the fortress interior is mostly empty and the causeway becomes a slow shuffle when a cruise ship is in.
onward: İzmir (ADB) then 1 hr 15 to Kuşadası; the causeway starts at the southern end of the seafront promenade, a 10-minute walk from the port

name: Dilek Peninsula National Park
tr: Dilek Yarımadası-Büyük Menderes Deltası Milli Parkı
desc: A forested ridge running out into the Aegean opposite Samos, with four pebble coves on the north side — İçmeler, Aydınlık, Kavaklıburun, Karasu — reached by one road through pine and wild olive. Wild boar cross it at dusk. The far end is a military zone, which is exactly why the water is so clear.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — swimmable Jun–Sep, but weekends in August are gridlocked
tip: Arrive before nine or the park hits its vehicle quota and shuts the gate; alternatively leave the car in Güzelçamlı and take the shuttle or bicycle in.
wiki: Dilek Peninsula-Büyük Menderes Delta National Park
todo: Watch for wild boar at dusk
rev: Repeatedly described as the cleanest water near Kuşadası, with two constant complaints: the entrance queue on summer weekends and boar that raid unattended picnic bags.
entry: Per-person park fee plus a vehicle charge — roughly ₺200–400 (≈€5–10) per car, cash easiest
onward: İzmir (ADB) then 1 hr 30 via Kuşadası and Güzelçamlı; the 'Milli Park' dolmuş runs from Kuşadası in summer

name: Cave of Zeus
desc: A collapsed karst chamber right beside the national park gate, filled with cold spring water that meets the sea underground, so it reads green at the edges and near-black in the middle. It is small — twenty metres across — and the shock when you get in is the whole experience. Fig roots hang down the rock.
season: Jun–Sep to swim; the water stays cold all year
tip: Go at opening time or after five; between eleven and four it is a queue of people photographing each other on the same ledge, and swimming is often stopped when it is busy.
todo: Swim in the cold spring pool
Tea at the stalls by the entrance
rev: Worth ten minutes for the colour of the water, but almost everyone says it is far smaller than the photographs suggest and mobbed in season, with slippery rock and no real changing space.
entry: Small fee — check locally; usually included if you are already paying to enter the national park
onward: İzmir (ADB) then 1 hr 30 to Güzelçamlı; the cave is signposted 200 m before the national park entrance gate

name: Güzelçamlı
desc: The last village before the national park gate: one long street of pensions, a Sunday market under plane trees, and grilled sardines eaten at plastic tables with the mountain behind. It is where people who want Dilek without Kuşadası prices stay, and it still shuts down properly in winter.
season: May–Oct — most pensions and half the restaurants close Nov–Mar
tip: The Sunday pazar is the real one for this coast — figs, thyme honey, village cheese — and it is over by two, so come early and eat gözleme at the far end.
rev: Praised as calmer and cheaper than Kuşadası with genuinely good fish, though the beach in the village itself is narrow and busy and traffic backs up on park-entry mornings.
onward: İzmir (ADB) then 1 hr 30; dolmuşes run every 20 minutes from Kuşadası bus station in season

name: Panionion
desc: The federal sanctuary where the twelve Ionian cities met, on a low hill of scrub and olive above Güzelçamlı. What survives is a rock-cut semicircular assembly place, eleven rows of seats hacked straight out of the hillside, and a view down the whole Ionian coast. There is nobody here, ever.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — grass and thistles swallow the seats by midsummer
tip: The turning is an unmarked farm track off the Güzelçamlı road near Otomatik; set the pin before you leave the village because there is no sign and no phone signal on the hill.
todo: Sit in the rock-cut assembly seats
rev: Those who find it call it the most atmospheric empty site in Ionia; most of the complaints are simply about failing to find it, since the access track is unsigned and rutted.
onward: İzmir (ADB) then 1 hr 30 to Güzelçamlı; from the village it is 3 km on a rough track best done on foot or in a high car

name: Karacasu
desc: A hill town of tiled roofs and timber-framed houses that has made red earthenware for centuries; the potters' quarter still turns and fires by hand, and the local speciality is a wide unglazed casserole. Add the Sunday market, a couple of old coffee houses and the fact that Aphrodisias is fifteen minutes up the road.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter is cold and grey up here
tip: Ask for the çömlekçiler mahallesi rather than the shops on the main road; the workshops sell the same pots at a third of the price and will fire a piece while you wait.
todo: Watch a potter throw a güveç
Ottoman houses on the upper streets
rev: Travellers who stop on the way to Aphrodisias are surprised by how intact the old town is; the recurring gripe is that several workshops are closed on Mondays and the town has little accommodation.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hr 45, or İzmir (ADB) 2 hr 30; the town is on the road between the Aydın–Denizli motorway and Aphrodisias

name: Nysa on the Maeander
desc: A city built astride a gorge, with a 100-metre Roman tunnel-bridge carrying the torrent under the centre — you can still walk into the mouth of it. Above are a library standing two storeys high, a theatre with hunting reliefs on the stage front, and olive terraces climbing to Mount Messogis behind.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the gorge is slippery after rain
tip: Go down to the stadium end and look back up into the tunnel arch; almost everyone stops at the theatre and misses the piece of engineering that makes the site unique.
rev: Visitors are impressed by the library and the tunnel and consistently note that signage is thin, the paths are overgrown in summer and the ticket office is sometimes unstaffed.
onward: İzmir (ADB) about 2 hours, or Denizli (DNZ) 1 hr 30; Sultanhisar is on the Aydın–Denizli road and the İZBAN-style regional train stops there

name: Çine Valley Road
desc: The road south from Çine follows the Çine Çayı — the ancient Marsyas — into a granite gorge where the river runs green between boulders the size of cars. Oleander lines the water, plane trees shade the roadside tea stops, and the rock walls close in until the Muğla plateau opens out at the top.
season: Apr–Jun for full water and green; the river drops to a trickle by August
tip: Pull in at one of the riverside kır lokantası between Çine and Eskiçine and ask for alabalık; they cook the trout over wood and the tables sit on platforms over the water.
todo: Trout lunch on a river platform
Detour to Alabanda on the way
rev: Drivers rate it one of the better back roads in the Aegean, though it carries heavy lorry traffic to Muğla and the dam upstream has visibly cut the river's flow.
onward: İzmir (ADB) or Bodrum (BJV), then the D525 south from Aydın through Çine towards Yatağan; the whole gorge is under an hour of driving

name: Kuyucak Lavender Fields
desc: A farming district in the upper Meander valley where growers have put lavender in among the figs and olives on the slopes towards Başaran and Pamukören. In late June the terraces go purple in stripes against grey olive, the air is loud with bees, and there is no ticket booth and no coach park.
season: Late Jun–mid Jul for the flower; the rest of the year it is a working fig district
tip: This is not the famous lavender village of the same name in Isparta; here the fields are scattered on private land, so ask at a village tea house before walking into a plot.
todo: Buy dried figs at the co-op
rev: Those who come for the purple photographs are sometimes disappointed to find the plantings smaller and more scattered than in Isparta, but nobody complains about crowds or fees.
onward: İzmir (ADB) about 2 hours or Denizli (DNZ) 1 hour; Kuyucak sits on the Aydın–Denizli road and the regional train stops in the town

name: Tralleis
desc: Three colossal brick arches — the Üç Gözler, the vaults of a Roman gymnasium — standing on the terrace directly above Aydın city, visible from the whole plain. The rest of the city is trenches, foundations and a long view over fig orchards to the Meander. It takes twenty minutes and reframes the town below.
season: Oct–May — the terrace is exposed and Aydın regularly tops 40 °C in summer
tip: The site sits inside a military zone boundary and opening has been erratic for years; phone the Aydın museum the day before rather than driving up on spec.
todo: Stand under the Üç Gözler arches
Finds in the Aydın museum afterwards
rev: The arches impress everyone who gets in; the repeated complaint is exactly that — access has been restricted or closed for long stretches and there is little to see beyond them.
entry: Free when open — access can be restricted, check with Aydın Archaeological Museum
onward: İzmir (ADB) about 1 hr 30 by motorway; from Aydın centre it is a 3 km climb north, easiest by taxi

name: Alinda
desc: Ada of Caria's stronghold, where she adopted Alexander, hanging above the village of Karpuzlu. A three-storey Hellenistic market building stands nearly complete with its barrel vaults intact, and the theatre looks straight out over the plain. Goats use the agora. It is one of the best-preserved Carian towns and almost nobody goes.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — thorny scrub and snakes make July a poor choice
tip: Walk uphill through the village to the agora first, then follow the wall line to the watchtower on the ridge; the theatre is signposted but the market hall is the reason to come.
rev: Visitors describe it as unfenced, unstaffed and wonderful, with the caveats that the last road is narrow and winding, there is no water on site and the grass hides loose stone.
onward: İzmir (ADB) or Bodrum (BJV), then the Çine road and 25 km west to Karpuzlu; a car is effectively required

name: Alabanda
desc: Fallen columns of an Ionic temple lying in an olive grove exactly where the earthquake dropped them, drum against drum, with a bouleuterion's walls standing to head height nearby. Cotton fields run right up to the ruins and a tractor track cuts through the middle. The Romans called it a town of scorpions and luxury.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the grove floods in winter and bakes in August
tip: Come after olive harvest in late autumn when the ground is cleared; in spring the undergrowth is waist-high and you will walk past the temple without seeing it.
todo: Toppled temple columns in the grove
rev: A quiet, unfenced pleasure for anyone who likes ruins without railings, though there is no signage, no facilities and the access lane through the village is easy to miss.
onward: İzmir (ADB) or Bodrum (BJV), then the D525 to Çine and 8 km north to Doğanyurt village; park at the village and walk in

name: Magnesia on the Maeander
desc: A site being pulled out of the mud year by year: the stadium was fully excavated only recently and its long banks of seating now run clear for two hundred metres. Add the Temple of Artemis Leukophryene's scattered frieze blocks and a theatre still half buried. Diggers work through the summer and you can watch.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the water table is high and parts flood in winter
tip: It is on the main Söke road with a proper car park, so it makes an easy 40-minute stop between Ephesus and Priene rather than a trip of its own.
rev: People are struck by the newly cleared stadium and equally struck by how much of the rest is still under earth, with muddy paths and minimal shade or explanation.
onward: İzmir (ADB) about 1 hr 15; the site is directly on the Selçuk–Söke road near Ortaklar and any Söke bus passes the gate

name: Pamukkale
desc: A white calcite hillside 160 metres high, built up over millennia by hot springs depositing lime, with terraced pools you walk through barefoot in warm shin-deep water. Only a strip of the terraces is open and the flow is rotated between them, so half the cascade is usually dry chalk rather than blue basins.
season: Apr–May and Oct — winter is cold on wet bare feet, August is a queue in 38 °C
tip: Enter at the lower south gate and walk up the travertines against the flow at sunrise, or arrive after four for the sunset light; midday is when every tour bus from the coast unloads.
todo: Barefoot walk up the terrace channel
Swim in the Antique Pool over sunken columns
rev: The colour genuinely delivers at the right hour, but visitors regularly report dry terraces, compulsory bare feet on sharp calcite, drone bans and a ticket price that has risen sharply.
entry: ≈€35 combined with Hierapolis · Antique Pool ≈€25 extra · Museum Pass covers the site but not the pool
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hour by road, or the İzmir–Denizli train then a 20-minute dolmuş from Denizli otogar

name: Hierapolis
desc: The Roman spa city on top of the travertines, and much larger than people expect: a theatre with its stage building restored to full height and carved friezes of Apollo, a colonnaded main street a kilometre long, and a necropolis of some twelve hundred tombs spread over the ridge to the north.
season: Apr–May and Oct — the plateau is shadeless and brutal Jul–Aug
tip: Walk north past the Martyrium of St Philip to the necropolis; it is twenty minutes from the crowds and you will usually have twelve hundred tombs to yourself.
todo: Necropolis walk to the north gate
Plutonium gas vent by the Apollo temple
rev: Often the surprise of the trip for people who came only for the white terraces; the standard complaints are the distances between monuments, no shade, and a museum in the Roman baths that closes earlier than the site.
entry: ≈€35 combined with Pamukkale · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hour; dolmuşes run from Denizli otogar to Pamukkale village every 20 minutes and the north gate is a taxi ride from there

name: Laodicea on the Lycus
desc: One of the seven churches of Revelation, and now the largest active excavation in the region: a re-erected colonnaded street with the water pipes still in the pavement, two theatres cut into the hillside, and a fourth-century basilica under a modern shelter with its opus sectile floor intact.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade at all on the plateau in summer
tip: Go for the covered Church of Laodicea first thing; the shelter is locked outside main hours and the mosaic floor is the single best thing on site.
todo: Fourth-century church floor under the shelter
rev: Biblical-tour groups and archaeology enthusiasts both rate it highly, while general visitors find it flat, hot and hard to read, and note the on-site café is minimal.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 50 minutes; the site is 6 km north of Denizli centre on the Pamukkale road, easiest by taxi or car

name: Colossae
desc: A grass-covered mound in a field below Honaz, with a theatre hollow you can trace by eye and potsherds turning up in the ploughed earth. Paul wrote a letter to the people who lived here and essentially nothing has been dug. What you get is the shape of a city and Mount Honaz filling the sky behind it.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the track is mud after rain
tip: Climb the höyük for the view rather than expecting ruins; the visible cut of the theatre is on the north slope facing the Lycus, and it is easiest to find in the low light of early morning.
todo: Honaz mountain view from the top
rev: Pilgrims come for the name and often leave disappointed because there is literally nothing built to see; those who treat it as a walk in a field with a good view are the ones who enjoy it.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 45 minutes; 3 km north-west of Honaz town on a signposted farm road, car needed

name: Kaklık Cave
desc: An underground Pamukkale: a collapsed cave whose floor is covered in miniature white travertine terraces filled with warm sulphurous water, lit from a hole in the roof. It is about the size of a tennis court, smells strongly of sulphur, and you walk it on a raised boardwalk in fifteen minutes.
season: All year — the cave holds a steady temperature and is a genuine winter option
tip: Bring nothing you mind smelling of sulphur, and combine it with Laodicea on the same morning; the cave is a 20-minute detour off the Denizli–Afyon road.
todo: Look up through the collapse hole
Warm sulphur pools at the far end
rev: Called a fair miniature of Pamukkale for a fraction of the price, with regular complaints about the smell, slippery boards, weak lighting and how quickly the visit is over.
entry: Small fee — check locally; municipal ticket, cash only
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 30 minutes; on the D320 towards Dinar, 40 km from Denizli centre, no useful public transport

name: Mount Honaz
desc: At 2,571 m the highest peak in the Aegean region, rising straight off the Lycus plain in one 2,000-metre wall. A national park road climbs through black pine and cedar to alpine meadow, and from the ridge you see Pamukkale's white scar, Lake Acıgöl and, on a clear day, the Bey mountains.
season: Jun–Oct for the summit; snow closes the upper road roughly Dec–Apr
tip: Start from Karateke picnic area rather than Honaz town — it cuts about 700 m of climbing — and carry all your water, because the springs on the ridge dry up by July.
rev: Hikers rate the summit view as one of the best in western Türkiye and warn that the ascent is long, unmarked in places, and that the forest road is rough and gated in winter.
entry: Small national park fee — check locally; usually charged per vehicle at the forest gate
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 45 minutes to Honaz, then a forest road up to the park; four-wheel drive is helpful above the picnic areas

name: Buldan
desc: A weaving town on a wooded slope above the Meander, with several hundred restored timber and stone houses on stepped lanes, and looms still working behind shop fronts. The cloth — loose crinkled cotton scarves and shawls — is the local trade, and above the town the Süleymanlı highland has a lake and cool pine.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the old town is steep and icy in winter
tip: Go up to Süleymanlı Yaylası for lunch after the old town; it is fifteen minutes of hairpins and around ten degrees cooler than the valley in summer.
todo: Old Buldan houses on the upper lanes
Buy crinkle-cotton cloth from a loom shop
rev: Visitors like the restored streets and cheap, genuine textiles; the recurring notes are that many houses are still derelict, parking is impossible in the old core and much of the town shuts on Sunday.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hr 15; Buldan is 45 minutes north-west of Denizli off the Aydın motorway, with regular buses from Denizli otogar

name: Babadağ
desc: A textile town clinging to a mountainside at 1,100 m, its houses stacked so steeply that one street's roofs are the next street's terraces. It is cold, quiet and unvisited, with plane-tree squares, spring water taps everywhere and a view straight down onto the Denizli plain and its lights at night.
season: May–Oct — the road up is snowbound in parts of winter
tip: Do not confuse it with Babadağ above Fethiye, which is the paragliding one; this Babadağ is a working town two hours away in the wrong direction if you booked a flight.
todo: Drink from the mountain spring taps
Night view over the Denizli plain
rev: Those who make the climb describe an unusually intact hill town with real daily life and almost no tourism, alongside warnings about the narrow hairpin road and very limited places to eat or sleep.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hr 15; 35 km south-west of Denizli on a steep mountain road, with a few daily minibuses from Denizli otogar

name: Lake Işıklı
desc: A shallow reed lake at the head of the Meander, fed by karst springs so clear you can see the sand boiling at the source. Fishermen work it from flat-bottomed boats for crayfish and carp, pelicans and flamingos use it on passage, and the village of Işıklı sits on a mound above the water with a ruined citadel.
season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov for birds; midsummer is hot, hazy and full of reeds
tip: Ask at the fish co-operative in Işıklı village about going out with a boat at dawn — it costs little and is the only way to see the spring welling up in the middle.
todo: Dawn boat over the karst springs
Bird hides on the northern reeds
rev: Birdwatchers and anglers rate it, general visitors find the shore muddy, reedy and short on facilities, and everyone notes that water levels and bird numbers vary a lot year to year.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 45 minutes; the lake is beyond Çivril, roughly 1 hr 30 from Denizli centre by car

name: Tripolis on the Meander
desc: A city on the river frontier between Lydia, Caria and Phrygia, excavated only in the last fifteen years and already showing a colonnaded street, a bath-basilica and a remarkable early Byzantine house with painted walls and its mosaic floors lifted and relaid. Cotton fields run to the edge of the trenches.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — flat, treeless and 40 °C in high summer
tip: It is signposted off the Denizli–Sarayköy road at Yenicekent and free; ask the guard to unlock the covered house with the wall paintings, which is not always open by default.
todo: City walls above the river terrace
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find the new digs genuinely exciting; casual visitors report an active building site with fencing, few explanatory panels and irregular opening.
entry: Free at present — a ticket booth has been built, so expect a small fee
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hour; on the Denizli–Buldan road at Yenicekent, 40 km from Denizli, car recommended

name: Akhan Caravanserai
desc: A Seljuk han of 1253 in white marble on the old road east out of Denizli, with a carved portal, an open courtyard and a covered hall of pointed arches behind it. Lions and rosettes are cut into the doorway. It is small, complete, free, and sits on a roundabout that almost everyone drives past.
season: All year — the covered hall is cool in summer and dry in winter
tip: The gate keeper's hours are loose; if the outer door is shut, walk round to the eastern side where the courtyard wall is low enough to see the whole plan.
rev: People are pleased to find a genuinely intact Seljuk han for nothing, and equally quick to say it takes twenty minutes, sits beside a busy road and is occasionally locked without warning.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 40 minutes; 7 km east of Denizli centre on the old Afyon road, any Honaz-bound dolmuş passes it

name: Güney Waterfall
desc: Water dropping about thirty metres over a mossy travertine lip into a green plunge pool, with a stepped path that takes you behind the curtain into the hollow under the rock. The gorge below is thick with fig and plane, and the spray keeps the whole amphitheatre cold even in August.
season: Mar–Jun for full flow; irrigation draws it down badly by late summer
tip: Take the lower path that ducks behind the fall rather than only viewing from the terrace café; the steps are wet and unrailed in places, so proper shoes matter.
todo: Plunge pool from the lower terrace
rev: Locals treat it as a summer picnic spot and rate it; travellers report litter around the picnic tables, a much reduced flow in late summer and a slippery unfenced descent.
entry: Free · small parking charge in season
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 1 hour; Güney is roughly 70 km north of Denizli via Çal, car needed as buses are infrequent

name: Bodrum
desc: White cubic houses with bougainvillea running down to two bays either side of the castle, a gulet harbour on one and the bar street on the other. The old town keeps its shape: sponge divers' lanes, the Sunday market, Halikarnas Balıkçısı's house. It is loud in August and quietly Mediterranean in May.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August is heat, traffic and peak prices
tip: Stay on the west bay near the castle rather than Cumhuriyet Caddesi; the bar street runs until four in the morning and the noise carries across the water.
todo: Sunday market in the old town
Gulet day trip from the marina
Sunset drink on the west bay
rev: Visitors love the castle, the harbour and the food, and complain consistently about August crowds, aggressive restaurant touts on the harbour front and cruise-day congestion in the bazaar.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) 35 km, about 45 minutes by Havaş shuttle or taxi; ferries run to Kos year-round and to Datça in summer

name: Bodrum Castle
desc: The Knights of St John built it from 1402 partly out of the Mausoleum's marble, and its towers still carry the coats of arms of English, French, German and Italian knights. Inside is the Museum of Underwater Archaeology, whose Uluburun shipwreck gallery holds a Bronze Age cargo of copper ingots, ivory and gold.
season: All year — the ramparts are exposed and hot Jul–Aug, superb in spring
tip: Go straight to the Uluburun and Glass Wreck halls when you enter; they are ticketed separately in practice and close earlier than the castle grounds.
rev: Consistently called the best museum on the Aegean coast, with the caveats that several galleries have been shut for restoration for years and the combined ticket costs more than people expect.
entry: ≈€25 · Museum Pass Türkiye covers entry; some special galleries carry a surcharge
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) 45 minutes by shuttle; the castle is on the harbour in the town centre, walkable from anywhere in Bodrum

name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
desc: A rectangular pit two streets back from the harbour, a few green-marble column drums, a sarcophagus fragment and the foundation of the tomb that gave every mausoleum its name. The Knights quarried it flat and the sculpture is in London. What remains is the outline, a scale model, and a strong sense of loss.
season: All year — the site is small and mostly open ground, best in spring light
tip: See the model and the wall panels first, then walk to the castle and look for the green volcanic stone from the Mausoleum reused in its walls; that connection is the real story.
rev: Visitors respect the history but are frank that one of the Seven Wonders is now a hole in the ground with a garden, and that the fee feels high for twenty minutes.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) 45 minutes; the site is a 10-minute uphill walk from the harbour on Turgutreis Caddesi

name: Theatre of Halicarnassus
desc: A fourth-century BC theatre cut into the hill above Bodrum, restored enough to still be used for concerts, with thirteen thousand seats looking straight down over the white town, the castle and the bay. It is free, it is open late in summer, and almost no one climbs up here in daylight.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the stone radiates heat in midsummer afternoons
tip: Walk up for the last half hour of daylight; the whole peninsula turns orange from the top row and it is the best free view in Bodrum.
todo: Top-row view over castle and bay
rev: Rated highly by those who find it, with two consistent notes: it sits beside a busy main road so the traffic noise carries, and modern restoration has replaced a lot of the seating.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) 45 minutes; from the harbour it is a steep 20-minute walk up Kıbrıs Şehitleri Caddesi, or a short taxi

name: Pedasa
desc: A Lelegian hill town above Konacık, reached by a walking track through scrub oak and thyme: cyclopean walls, a tower, rock-cut tombs and a sanctuary of Athena, all at 400 m with the whole Bodrum peninsula laid out beneath. Herodotus wrote about the priestess here who grew a beard before disasters.
season: Oct–May — the hillside is tinder-dry and snake-warm in high summer
tip: Start from the Gökçeler track above Konacık in the cool of the morning; it is 40 minutes up on a rough path with no water and no shade at the top.
rev: Hikers rate the walk and the silence; the constant complaint is that the trail is poorly marked, easy to lose in scrub, and that the ruins themselves are modest if you are not into Carian archaeology.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 35 minutes to Konacık, then the unpaved track towards Gökçeler; the last stretch is on foot

name: Gümüşlük and Myndos
desc: A fishing village at the peninsula's western tip where the ancient city of Myndos lies half underwater — you can wade the submerged causeway to Rabbit Island in knee-deep water over cut stone. Building is restricted because of the ruins, so the bay has stayed low, and the fish restaurants sit with their feet in the sea.
season: Jun–Sep for wading and swimming; May and Oct for the village without the queue
tip: Wade to the island barefoot before dinner and eat late, after the sunset rush; the causeway stones are sharp, so reef shoes save the evening.
todo: Wade the sunken causeway to Rabbit Island
Sunset fish dinner on the water
Ancient walls and harbour under the surface
rev: Widely called the most attractive corner of the peninsula, with two complaints repeated everywhere: restaurant prices well above the Bodrum average and a village that is thoroughly full on August evenings.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 55 minutes by road; dolmuşes run from Bodrum otogar via Turgutreis, and parking in the village is limited

name: Yalıkavak
desc: A former sponge-diving village turned superyacht marina, where hundred-metre boats moor a few streets from a whitewashed old quarter of windmills and stone lanes. The abandoned Greek village of Sandıma sits on the slope above, roofless and quiet, and the wild Küdür headland to the west has coves with nobody on them.
season: Jun–Sep for the sea; May and Oct for the village and the walks
tip: Walk up to Sandıma in the late afternoon — twenty minutes above the marina — then come down for dinner; it is free, empty, and the contrast with the yachts below is the point.
todo: Sandıma ghost village on the hill
rev: People rate the marina restaurants and the old streets, then note that prices in the yacht marina are Monaco-level and that the village beach itself is small and pebbly.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 50 minutes; regular dolmuşes from Bodrum otogar take 30 minutes over the ridge

name: Gündoğan
desc: A deep north-facing bay with a long shallow beach, tangerine gardens behind it, and a headland at the western end where a cave church with Byzantine frescoes is cut into the cliff above the water. Quieter than Türkbükü across the ridge, and the fish restaurants are aimed at Turkish families rather than club crowds.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; the meltemi blows hardest across this north coast in July
tip: Take a small boat or kayak from the beach to the Manastır cave on the west point — it is only reachable from the water and most people staying here never see it.
todo: Cave church on the western headland
Long shallow swim off the main beach
rev: Regulars value the calm and the value for money compared with Türkbükü; the common gripes are strong afternoon wind, a beach that narrows in front of the hotels and thin nightlife.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 40 minutes; dolmuşes from Bodrum otogar run every half hour in season

name: Türkbükü
desc: The peninsula's fashionable bay, where there is barely any sand and the beach is instead a chain of wooden decks built out over the water, each belonging to a club or hotel. Boats anchor in rows, the İstanbul crowd arrives in July, and the mandarin groves behind still smell of the village it used to be.
season: Jun–Sep — everything worth eating at is shut Nov–Apr
tip: There is almost no free public shore here; check the daily deck minimum spend before you sit down, because a sunbed on a name platform costs more than dinner elsewhere.
todo: Swim off a wooden deck platform
rev: People come for the scene and the water quality and report exactly the expected downside: high minimum spends, no real beach, and a road behind the bay that jams solid in August.
entry: Free to the village · beach decks charge a daily minimum spend
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 35 minutes, the closest of the peninsula bays to the airport; dolmuşes run from Bodrum otogar

name: Bitez
desc: A south-facing bay backed by one of the last big tangerine groves on the peninsula, with a shallow sandy shore, a shaded promenade under trees, and enough steady afternoon breeze that it became the windsurfing bay. Five kilometres from Bodrum and a completely different pace once the sun drops.
season: Jun–Sep for the water; the wind is reliable Jun–Aug for boards
tip: Walk the coastal path east from the bay towards Bodrum for twenty minutes to reach small unmarked rock coves that never fill up.
todo: Coast path east to the rock coves
rev: Families and windsurfers both rate it, and both mention the same things: the water is very shallow a long way out, sea grass washes up on the sand, and the strip is dominated by all-inclusive hotels.
entry: Free · sunbed hire on the organised sections
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 40 minutes; dolmuşes from Bodrum otogar take 15 minutes and run late in season

name: Akyarlar
desc: The peninsula's south-western corner, with fine pale sand, Kos sitting close enough across the strait to see cars on it, and the conical hill of Aspat — the Byzantine fortress of Strobilos — rising behind the bay. A row of low fish restaurants, a small mosque, and none of the Bodrum noise.
season: Jun–Oct — the sea here stays warm latest on the peninsula
tip: Climb Aspat hill from the eastern side in the last hour of light; it is a 30-minute scramble to the fortress and the view down the Kos strait is the best on this coast.
rev: Regulars call it the best sand on the peninsula and the calmest village left; the recurring notes are limited shade, a long drive from Bodrum and very little to do after dinner.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 1 hour via Turgutreis; dolmuşes run from Bodrum otogar through Turgutreis to Akyarlar

name: Karaincir
desc: A single crescent of coarse pale sand between two headlands on the south coast, sheltered from the meltemi, with water that shelves gently and a handful of low pensions behind the tamarisks. It is the beach Bodrum locals drive to on their own day off, and it is still mostly Turkish families.
season: Jun–Oct — sheltered from the north wind, so it works when the north coast is choppy
tip: Park at the far eastern end near the tamarisks rather than the central car park; that section has no sunbed operator and you can put a towel straight on the sand.
todo: Swim in the sheltered crescent bay
Grilled fish at a beach shack
rev: Praised for calm, clean water and low prices; the complaints are that sunbeds now cover much of the sand, the road in is narrow and the beach fills completely on summer weekends.
entry: Free · sunbed hire on the organised stretch
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 1 hour; take the Turgutreis road then the Akyarlar turning, or the Akyarlar dolmuş from Bodrum otogar

name: Labraunda
desc: The Carian sanctuary of Zeus Labraundos, on a pine terrace at 600 m reached by fourteen kilometres of switchbacks above Milas. Two andrones — banqueting halls built by Maussollos and his brother — still stand to roof height, there is a sacred spring house, and a Sacred Way once ran all the way down to the city.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the road ices over in winter and the site is cold
tip: The last few kilometres are steep and narrow with no barrier; go up in the morning, because meeting a logging lorry on the descent in poor light is genuinely unpleasant.
todo: Andron A and B standing walls
rev: Those who make the drive call it the most atmospheric Carian site anywhere, and every account warns about the mountain road, the lack of any facilities and a guard who may or may not be there.
entry: Small fee — check locally; often unstaffed and free in practice
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 40 minutes to Milas, then 14 km of mountain road north; no public transport, car essential

name: Euromos
desc: Sixteen Corinthian columns of a temple of Zeus standing in an olive grove fifty metres off the Milas–Söke road, several still carrying their architrave. Some shafts were never fluted because the donors stopped paying, and the inscriptions naming those donors are still legible on them. Ten minutes and one of the best-preserved temples in Anatolia.
season: All year — spring poppies in the grove make it, midsummer light is flat and harsh
tip: It is easy to shoot from the road and drive on; walk into the grove behind the temple instead, where the theatre and the city wall are hidden in the trees.
todo: Unfinished column shafts and donor names
rev: Everyone agrees it is remarkable value for a five-minute stop; the criticisms are the road noise from the adjacent highway and that the site takes almost no time to see.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 30 minutes; directly on the D525 Milas–Söke road, 12 km north of Milas, any Söke bus can drop you at the gate

name: Iasos
desc: A city on a near-island in the Gulf of Güllük, where the ancient breakwater still shelters fishing boats and the modern village of Kıyıkışlacık uses the agora as its back garden. There is a theatre facing the water, a Roman fish market rebuilt as a small museum, and swimming straight off the ruins.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the peninsula is exposed and hot in high summer
tip: Follow the track out to the isthmus and the necropolis on the far side; the sarcophagi sit right on the shore and you can swim from the rocks below them.
rev: Loved for the combination of ruins and sea and the total absence of coaches; the recurring notes are a rough 15 km access road, patchy opening hours and a village with only a couple of places to eat.
entry: Small fee — check locally; the site museum keeps shorter hours than the ruins
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 40 minutes; turn off the Milas–Güllük road at Kıyıkışlacık and follow it 16 km to the coast

name: Lake Bafa
desc: A former sea gulf cut off by the Meander's silt, now a brackish lake with granite islets carrying ruined Byzantine monasteries and the Beşparmak range rising straight out of the water behind it. Flamingos and pelicans work the shallows, and the light on those boulder mountains at dusk is the reason people stay.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov for birds and hiking; summer is hot and hazy, swimming is poor
tip: Stop at the lakeside restaurants on the old road at Kapıkırı rather than the ones on the new highway; ask for the lake's own fish, yayın or levrek, grilled over wood.
rev: Photographers and birdwatchers rate it very highly; visitors expecting a swimming lake are disappointed by the salinity, the muddy shore and the highway that runs along the northern edge.
entry: Free · boat trips to the islands negotiated at Kapıkırı
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 50 minutes, or İzmir (ADB) 2 hr 15; the D525 Milas–Söke road runs along the lake's north shore

name: Herakleia under Latmos
desc: The village of Kapıkırı is built inside the ancient city: houses stand between a temple of Athena on its rock, a bouleuterion, and a Hellenistic wall that runs six kilometres up the mountain. Sarcophagi lie half submerged at the lake edge, and goats graze the agora. Granite boulders the size of houses are everywhere.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — perfect walking weather; July is airless among the rocks
tip: Stay a night in one of the village pensions; the day-trippers leave by five and the temple rock at sunset over the lake is what you actually came for.
todo: Temple of Athena on its rock
Walk a stretch of the Hellenistic wall
rev: Repeatedly described as one of the most extraordinary places in western Türkiye, with honest warnings about the rough 10 km approach road, a village entry charge collected informally, and persistent pressure to buy scarves and boat trips.
entry: Small village fee — check locally; the ruins themselves are open ground
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 1 hour; turn north off the D525 at Çamiçi and follow 10 km of narrow road to Kapıkırı

name: Latmos Rock Paintings
desc: On the Beşparmak massif above Lake Bafa, prehistoric painters left red ochre figures on the undersides of granite overhangs — human couples, hands, dancing groups — dated to roughly six thousand BC and unlike anything else in Anatolia. The rock itself, weathered into stacked spheres and caves, is half the experience.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the granite is an oven in summer and there is no shade
tip: You will not find the shelters alone; hire a guide from Kapıkırı or Gölyaka, which costs little and is the difference between seeing paintings and seeing boulders.
todo: Ochre figures under the granite overhangs
Byzantine monastery ruins on the slopes
rev: Those who go with a guide describe it as unforgettable; the complaints are all about access — unmarked paths, some sites damaged by graffiti and quarrying, and paintings that are faint unless the light is right.
entry: Free · guide fee negotiated in the village, roughly ₺1000–1500 (≈€25–35) for a half day
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 1 hour to Çamiçi on the D525, then the Kapıkırı or Gölyaka road; walking access only beyond the villages

name: Beçin Castle
desc: The Menteşe emirs' capital on a flat rock plateau above Milas: a walled castle, and outside it a whole abandoned medieval town of madrasas, baths, a mosque and Ahmet Gazi's tomb, spread over the tableland among wild olives. The cliff edge drops straight to the Milas plain.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plateau is completely exposed in summer
tip: The castle is only half of it; walk 300 m beyond the walls to the Ahmet Gazi Medresesi and the Bey Hamamı, which are unfenced, free and better preserved than the fortress.
todo: Ahmet Gazi madrasa outside the gate
rev: Visitors find it an unexpectedly large and evocative medieval site, and note the sparse signage, the long walk between scattered monuments and a site that is fully open to the sun.
entry: Small fee — check locally; covered by Museum Pass Türkiye when the booth is staffed
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 35 minutes; 5 km south of Milas on the Ören road, signposted from the Milas ring road

name: Milas
desc: The old Carian capital Mylasa, now a market town with a Roman tomb called Gümüşkesen standing complete in a back street, the Firuz Bey Mosque of 1394 in blue-grey marble, and a Tuesday bazaar that fills the whole centre. Carpets from the surrounding villages are still woven and sold here.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the Tuesday market is the reason to time a visit
tip: Gümüşkesen is a fifteen-minute walk uphill from the bazaar and unstaffed; go there first while you have energy, then work back down through the market.
todo: Tuesday bazaar in the old centre
rev: Travellers passing to the airport are surprised by how much survives, while also reporting heavy traffic through the centre, poor parking and monuments that are scattered and often locked.
entry: Free · the small archaeological museum charges a nominal fee
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) is 15 minutes away, the closest town to the airport; buses run from Bodrum, Söke and Muğla to Milas otogar

name: Ören and Ceramus
desc: A quiet village on the north shore of the Gulf of Gökova with a long grey-pebble beach, and the ancient city of Ceramus scattered through the gardens behind it — a temple podium in an olive field, city walls in someone's orchard. Across the gulf the pine wall of the Datça road rises straight out of the sea.
season: Jun–Sep to swim; Apr–May and Oct for the ruins and the walking
tip: The ruins are not fenced or signed; ask in the village for the Zeus Chrysaoreus temple podium, which stands in a private olive grove and needs a nod from the owner.
todo: Swim off the long pebble beach
Find the temple podium in the olives
rev: Regulars value the near-total absence of tourism and the clear water; the drawbacks are a coarse pebble beach, a long winding drive from anywhere and a power station visible along the coast.
onward: Bodrum–Milas (BJV) about 1 hr 15; 45 km south of Milas on a mountain road via Beçin, with a few daily minibuses
